“You own it.” That sentence appears to settle the matter. Money changes hands, the box crosses the counter, and the device enters your home. But what exactly crossed the counter with it? A machine you control, or a machine whose most important powers remain rented from its maker?

The distinction matters because modern devices increasingly contain two things at once: hardware sitting in your hand and software waiting for permission. The hardware may be yours in the ordinary sense. The software can still decide what the hardware is allowed to do. If the maker can disable a feature after the sale, then the sale transferred possession while withholding control. That’s a strange kind of ownership (a deed with a remote-control clause hidden in the basement).

Of course, makers will say that remote disablement protects security, fixes defects, or responds to abuse. Sometimes it will. We should be able to repair a dangerous flaw, revoke a fraudulent service, or stop a device from causing immediate harm. But a narrow emergency power can become a general license to rewrite the bargain. Once the switch exists, you’re asked to trust the company’s judgment forever – including when its judgment conflicts with your own.

What happens when a feature you paid for becomes inconvenient to the business? What happens when the company changes its subscription, abandons support, or decides that your perfectly functional device belongs in the obsolete pile? The answer is already contained in the architecture: you can keep the object, but you can’t necessarily keep its capabilities.

I think we should call this what it is: conditional ownership. It resembles buying a house where the builder retains a key and reserves the right to remove a room whenever the economics change. You may paint the walls, carry in furniture, and pay the taxes, but the floor plan remains subject to somebody else’s approval. That isn’t ownership in the meaningful civic sense. It’s possession with a landlord hiding inside it.

The usual defense is that the terms were disclosed. Perhaps they were, in twelve pages of dense language displayed at the least memorable moment of a purchase. But disclosure can’t turn an unequal bargain into a fair one. If every major device comes with the same trap, “choice” becomes a polite word for surrender. We’ve been offered a market where every door has the same lock and every key belongs to the manufacturer.

This is where digital rights become physical rights. Your phone, car, thermostat, medical equipment, or tool isn’t merely a vessel for an online account. It occupies your space, consumes your money, and mediates your ability to act. When a remote command can erase a function, the maker has acquired a continuing power over your daily life. That power deserves limits – and those limits should attach to the sale, not to the company’s changing preferences.

I’m not arguing that every feature must remain frozen forever. Security updates should remain possible. A device that genuinely threatens someone should invite intervention. But the burden belongs with the maker: explain the danger, use the narrowest remedy, and preserve the buyer’s other lawful uses. Don’t call a permanent veto a safety feature. That’s bullshit, and we should recognize it when we hear it.

We can write a simple rule: after sale, a maker may maintain a device, but it may not casually withdraw what the buyer purchased. If a feature requires a continuing service, say so plainly before the transaction. If the feature lives in the device and formed part of its advertised value, you should own the ability to use it.

I’ve heard the argument that this would slow innovation. Maybe it would slow one kind: the kind that treats customers as temporary licensees and finished products as unfinished negotiations. We don’t need faster ways to lose control. We need devices that cross the counter with their promises intact.

Ownership means the maker’s hand leaves the object. If the hand remains on the switch, the sale hasn’t ended – and you’re still paying rent.
